description: We’re Axiom, five Computer Engineering students from Birzeit University: Leen, Shahd, Twaba, Duha, and Nidal. Our skills span AI, software, embedded systems, and cybersecurity. We're developing a wearable bracelet and sleeve that monitor astronauts’ health and provide early warnings during long missions. We're looking for teammates skilled in biomedical sciences, ML, UI/UX, electronics, or storytelling to help us build an innovative, working prototype!
summary: AstroVitals is a web app that lets an astronaut check their own health on a long mission, when Earth is minutes away and no doctor is aboard. One tap on "Measure vitals" reads a simulated wrist band, upper-arm blood pressure cuff and glucose patch, and shows each result with its quality, calibration and context. Out-of-range readings get a short recommendation and a "What to do now" list. A Mental check combines a five-question well-being survey with an on-device camera reaction test. A "Protect your fitness" card compares weekly training with NASA exercise guidance. Everything runs offline in the browser, queues records for Earth, and is labelled simulated data, not medical advice. It addresses the challenge by showing how a crew could track heart, sleep, nutrition, behavioral and exercise health on their own, with honest limits.
details:
What it does. The astronaut picks an account, taps Measure vitals, and gets six cards: heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, sleep and cabin air. Each card has a High, Normal or Low tag, and out-of-range ones add a short action. Sleep, Glucose and History are tabs, and an Earth page shows what the ground has received, including a Compare tab for on-board versus Earth readings. A Coverage page lists what the device measures and does not, by NASA health area.

Honesty by design. Every reading is labelled with its quality (good, motion, poor fit), calibration age and missing context. Ranges are marked as placeholders, and the app never states a diagnosis. The Mental check is labelled a screening aid.

How it works. A single in-browser simulation engine produces readings and runs a store-and-forward link to Earth. The Mental check runs pose and hand detection on the device, so no video is stored or sent. Replay mode can play recorded public data through the same pipeline.

Benefits and impact. It shows a way for crews to notice declines early and keep working when communication is delayed, and it keeps the data private on the device.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, MediaPipe Tasks Vision, IndexedDB, vitest (212 tests), and GitHub Pages hosting.

What we considered. Offline-first use, small uncluttered screens, and clear separation of simulated data from real data. Everything marked "needs review" (ranges, recommendation wording, survey cut-offs) must be checked by a flight surgeon before real use.

Limits. All crew and device data is simulated. This is a prototype, not a medical device.
